title: Salivary glands
description: Diseases of the major (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) and minor salivary glands — obstructive, infective, inflammatory, autoimmune, and neoplastic.

problems.description: Recurrent episodic unilateral parotid pain and swelling provoked by eating, relieved between meals.
problems.etiology: A stone forms inside the parotid duct and blocks outflow. The interesting bit is that a significant proportion of these calculi are radiolucent — so a clear plain film doesn't actually rule one out [1]. Sialography can pick up the obstruction even when plain X-rays look completely normal [2].
problems.presentation: The pattern is meal-triggered swelling. What happens is: eating stimulates salivary flow, flow meets the blocked duct, and pressure builds — producing pain and a tense swelling that then settles between meals [1]. It's episodic and recurrent.
problems.results: Plain X-rays of the cheek pick up radio-opaque calculi [1]. Sialography reveals the obstruction as a stricture or filling defect [2]. For proximal stones under 3 mm where the patient wants to avoid surgery, sialoendoscopy with laser lithotripsy is an option at specialist centres [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Eating-triggered parotid swelling that resolves between meals is the hallmark [1].
problems.treatment: Expose and lift out the stone directly via an intraoral approach for anterior duct calculi. For more posterior stones, place a probe in the duct first and raise a small skin flap onto it [4]. Deep or inaccessible stones need selective superficial parotidectomy — that's the only safe route [4]. Sialoendoscopy with laser lithotripsy for small proximal stones if the patient wants to stay conservative [3].
problems.prognosis: Remove the stone and the episodic swelling goes. Severe recurrent infection of the gland can lead to sialectasis — dilation and ballooning of the ducts [5].

citations.quote: History is of recurrent pain and swelling in the obstructed gland, particularly before and during meals. Plain X-rays (lower occlusal for submandibular, cheek for parotid) reveal radio-opaque calculi, but do not exclude the radiolucent calculi and mucous plugs.
Sialography reveals a stricture or obstruction.
Sialoendoscopy ± laser lithotripsy is available in some centres for proximal calculi in patients wishing to avoid gland excision and calculi <3mm.

Rx: parotid duct—expose duct via IO approach for anterior stones or via a small skin flap onto a probe in the duct for more posterior calculi. Otherwise, selective superficial parotidectomy is the only safe approach.
Severe recurrent infection of the parotid or submandibular glands leads to dilatation and ballooning of the ducts and alveoli called sialectasis.

problems.description: Painful unilateral major salivary gland swelling with purulent discharge from the duct opening.
problems.etiology: Bacteria ascend the duct, usually when outflow is impaired. The two common triggers are duct obstruction and systemic dehydration — the second one is why you see ascending parotid infection in elderly hospital inpatients who aren't drinking [1]. The organisms are mostly oral streptococci, oral anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus [1]. Chronic sialadenitis often runs as a background state on top of duct obstruction, flaring into acute episodes periodically [1].
problems.presentation: Painful swelling of one gland, almost always unilateral, with pus expressible from the duct opening [1]. The dehydrated elderly inpatient with a swollen parotid is a recognised scenario — easy to miss if you're not thinking about salivary glands [1].
problems.results: Plain films may show an obstructing stone, but 50% of calculi are radiolucent, so a clear film doesn't rule one out [1]. Culture the pus from the duct to identify the organism [1]. If there's a loculated collection inside the gland and you're considering incision and drainage, ultrasound localises it first [1]. Once the acute episode settles, sialography is indicated to define the duct anatomy — and can actually be therapeutic in the process [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Unilateral painful gland swelling with expressible pus from the duct is the diagnostic picture [1]. Both acute and chronic forms are almost always unilateral — bilateral involvement should make you think of something else [1].
problems.treatment: Rehydrate. Remove or exclude any obstructing stone [1]. Start co-amoxiclav, or amoxicillin with metronidazole — this covers the typical mixed flora [1]. Encourage salivary flow: chewing, massage. This is especially useful in chronic recurring cases [1]. Rarely, if pus is loculated inside the gland, you'll need incision and drainage [1]. Recurrent chronic sialadenitis that doesn't settle with conservative measures is an indication for gland removal [2].
problems.prognosis: Most acute episodes resolve with rehydration, antibiotics, and addressing the obstruction. Recurrent chronic sialadenitis is an indication for removal of the gland [2].

citations.quote: Acute bacterial sialadenitis presents as a painful swelling, usually with a purulent discharge from the duct of the gland involved. It may also develop as an exacerbation of chronic bacterial sialadenitis, which often exists as a complication of duct obstruction. Ascending infection of the parotid glands occurs in dehydrated elderly patients. Both acute and chronic conditions are almost always unilateral and common infecting organisms are oral streptococci, oral anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Rx: rehydration and exclusion or removal of an obstructing calculus. Plain radiographs may reveal calculus, but 50% are radiolucent. Culture of pus from the duct and aggressive antibiotic therapy (co-amoxiclav or amoxicillin and metronidazole). Stimulation of salivary flow by chewing or massage helps chronic recurring sialadenitis. Rarely, loculated pus collection within the gland necessitates incision and drainage; USS can localize collection. Once the acute symptoms have resolved, sialography is indicated to define duct structure and may prove therapeutic.
Recurrent chronic sialadenitis is an indication for removal of the gland.

problems.description: Acute bilateral parotid swelling with fever in a child or young adult; may have orchitis or meningitis in adults.
problems.etiology: Mumps is a paramyxoviral infection spread by saliva droplets [1]. It mainly targets the parotid glands — 10% of cases also involve the submandibular gland [1]. MMR vaccination largely keeps it at bay, but UK incidence has crept back up following reduced vaccine uptake driven by fraudulent and widely publicised research [1]. So the epidemiological context matters: unvaccinated individual, or an outbreak situation.
problems.presentation: Sudden-onset fever, pain, and parotid swelling. Classically one gland swells first, then the other follows — bilateral involvement is the norm [1]. The disease hits children and young adults hardest [1]. The reason it matters in adults is the complication profile: epididymo-orchitis, oophoritis, mastitis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, and meningoencephalitis are all on the table [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical. Bilateral parotid involvement, fever, and the absence of vaccination in an appropriate age group is the picture.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bilateral parotid swelling with fever in an unvaccinated patient — particularly a child or young adult — is the hallmark [1]. The adult complications, especially orchitis and meningitis, distinguish this from bacterial sialadenitis, which is unilateral and produces pus [1].
problems.treatment: Supportive management. Isolate the patient for 7–10 days to limit onward transmission [1].
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting in most. Adult men carry a genuine risk of epididymo-orchitis [1]. The takeaway: MMR vaccination protects against all of this — the cases you see now are largely a consequence of reduced vaccine uptake [1].

citations.quote: Viral sialadenitis, commonly mumps, is an acute, infectious paramyxoviral disease which primarily affects the parotid (10% submandibular gland). It is transmitted by direct contact with droplets of saliva and usually affects children and young adults with sudden onset of fever, pain, and parotid swelling. Classically, one gland is affected first, although bilateral swelling is the norm. In adults, the disease is more severe, with multisystem problems such as epididymo-orchitis, oophoritis/mastitis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, and meningoencephalitis. Protection is conferred by the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, however the incidence in the UK has ↑ following reduced vaccine intake 2° to fraudulent but highly publicized 'research'. Rx: supportive, isolate patient for 7–10 days.

problems.description: Dry mouth and dry eyes in a middle-aged woman, often alongside joint disease; raised risk of salivary lymphoma.
problems.etiology: An autoimmune attack on the salivary and lacrimal glands, reducing their secretory output [1]. About 90% of patients are women [1]. Secondary Sjögren syndrome is the triad of dry mouth, dry eyes, and a connective tissue disorder — most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, though SLE, systemic sclerosis, and primary biliary cholangitis all feature [1, 2]. When there's no connective tissue disease, you're looking at primary Sjögren syndrome (sicca syndrome) [1]. The reason this matters beyond the symptoms: there is a 5% risk of malignant lymphomatous transformation in the affected gland [1].
problems.presentation: Dry mouth and dry eyes are the cardinal symptoms [1, 3]. Actual gland swelling is uncommon — but when a patient with established Sjögren syndrome develops late-onset parotid swelling, that's a red flag for lymphoma [2]. Secondary cases also carry the systemic features of the associated connective tissue disease [2].
problems.results: Antinuclear antibodies positive in 70%, SSA in 70%, SSB in 40%, rheumatoid factor in 70%. ESR and immunoglobulins are raised [1]. Labial gland biopsy may show a lymphocytic infiltrate [1]. Saliva flowmetry, sialography, Schirmer test, and slit-lamp exam all have a role [1]. Diagnosis requires four positive findings from six categories: ocular symptoms, oral symptoms, ocular signs, histopathological features, salivary gland involvement, and autoantibodies [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Dry mouth plus dry eyes plus positive SSA/SSB autoantibodies in a woman with rheumatoid arthritis is the classic picture [1]. The 5% lymphoma risk is what makes this a condition you monitor long-term, not just manage symptomatically [1].
problems.treatment: Symptomatic management: synthetic saliva, synthetic tears, meticulous oral hygiene, treat oral candida promptly [1]. Make sure the patient understands the lymphoma risk — they need to report new gland swelling [1].
problems.prognosis: No cure. The dryness is managed indefinitely. The principal concern is that 5% lymphoma risk, so lifelong surveillance is part of the plan [1].

citations.quote: About 90% of patients with Sjögren syndrome are female. It comprises the triad of xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and a connective tissue disorder, usually rheumatoid arthritis. When the connective tissue component is absent the condition is called primary Sjögren syndrome (sicca syndrome). This is an autoimmune disease affecting salivary and lacrimal glands and causing a reduction of the secretion activity. The aetiology is probably autoimmune and there is a 5% risk of malignant lymphomatous transformation of the affected gland. ∆: antinuclear antibodies (70% +ve), SSA (70% +ve), SSB (40% +ve). Rheumatoid factor (70% +ve), ESR (i), immunoglobulins (i), labial gland biopsy may show lymphocytic infiltrate. Saliva flowmetry, sialography, Schirmer test, and slit lamp exam can be performed. Diagnosis is made on the basis of four positive findings out of the six categories which include ocular symptoms, oral symptoms, ocular signs, histopathological features, salivary gland involvement, and autoantibodies. Management is symptomatic Rx which may include synthetic saliva, synthetic tears, meticulous OH, Rx of candida, and patient awareness of the risk of lymphomatous change.

In addition to dry eyes and dry mouth this has both the serology and symptomatology of an autoimmune condition, usually rheumatoid arthritis, but sometimes SLE, systemic sclerosis, or 1° biliary cholangitis. Actual swelling of the salivary glands is relatively uncommon and late-onset swelling of the parotids may herald the presence of a lymphoma.
Xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, i.e. dry mouth and dry eyes. There is an ↑ risk of developing parotid lymphoma with this condition.

problems.description: Firm slow-growing swelling in the parotid region, present for years, with no pain or nerve involvement.
problems.etiology: The commonest benign salivary tumour — and the rule of 80s helps organise this: 80% of all salivary tumours are benign, 80% occur in the parotid, and 80% of parotid tumours are in the superficial lobe [1]. Pleomorphic adenomas make up the bulk of that group, and they have a mixed cellular appearance on histopathology [1]. The thing is, although these are benign, satellite cells can lie outside the tumour capsule — which means simple enucleation leaves residual disease behind and creates a high recurrence risk [1].
problems.presentation: A firm, slow-growing parotid mass. A long history without pain and without any facial nerve involvement strongly points to a benign lesion [2]. The features that flip the probability toward malignancy are: pain, facial nerve palsy, rapid growth, and size over 4 cm [2].
problems.results: History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools [2]. CT, fine-needle aspiration cytology, ultrasound, and MRI can all assist characterisation, especially when features are borderline or surgery is being planned [2]. The chance of malignancy rises significantly once the tumour exceeds 4 cm [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: A firm, mobile, slow-growing parotid mass in a middle-aged adult, present for years, with no facial nerve involvement — that's the classic picture [2]. What makes this tumour clinically important is the satellite-cell biology: they sit outside the capsule, so you can't just shell the tumour out [1].
problems.treatment: Formal parotidectomy or formal extracapsular dissection, taking a clear margin of normal tissue [1]. Simple enucleation is not acceptable — satellite cells outside the capsule make recurrence near-certain if you don't take a margin [1]. Preserve the facial nerve throughout [3].
problems.prognosis: A clear margin on formal parotidectomy gives good long-term control. Enucleation carries a high recurrence risk. Malignant transformation can occur in a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma, so this isn't a tumour to leave and watch [4].

citations.quote: About 80% are benign; 80% occur in the parotid and 80% of these are in the superficial lobe. The majority are pleomorphic salivary adenomas (PSAs) which have a mixed cellular appearance on histopathology. Although benign, the cells lie within the capsule of the tumour and satellite cells may lie outside the capsule, creating a tremendous propensity for recurrence if simply enucleated. A tumour in the parotid should therefore be removed by parotidectomy or at minimum formal extracapsular dissection, taking a safe margin of normal tissue if possible.

History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools. Long history, no pain, and no facial nerve involvement suggest benign tumour. Facial palsy, pain, and rapid growth suggest malignancy. Chance of malignancy much greater in tumours >4cm.
The principles are complete excision of a tumour with a margin of healthy tissue and preservation of facial nerve.
Other carcinomas are rare, but may arise in a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma or de novo.

problems.description: Soft fluctuant parotid swelling in an older male smoker; may be bilateral; slow-growing and cystic in feel.
problems.etiology: Warthin's tumour lives almost exclusively in the parotid — that's essentially a defining feature [1]. It affects men more than women, is rare under 50, and has a well-established association with smoking [1]. The interesting bit is the bilateral rate: about 10% of cases involve both parotids, which you won't see with most parotid tumours [1].
problems.presentation: A soft, cystic-feeling swelling in the parotid region — that softness is actually helpful diagnostically, because most parotid masses feel firm [1]. Slow-growing and benign. One in ten patients has bilateral involvement [1].
problems.results: History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: A soft, cystic parotid lump in an older male smoker — bilateral in 10% — is the hallmark [1]. Unlike pleomorphic adenoma, it doesn't carry a meaningful risk of malignant transformation, and recurrence after excision is very unlikely despite being multifocal [1].
problems.treatment: Surgical excision with facial nerve preservation [2]. All salivary gland tumours (except lymphomas) get surgery first [3].
problems.prognosis: Benign, low recurrence risk, no recognised risk of malignant transformation [1]. Contrast this with pleomorphic adenoma: Warthin's is the more reassuring diagnosis of the two common parotid tumours.

citations.quote: Monomorphic adenoma—adenolymphoma (Warthin's tumour) affects M > F; rare <50yrs. Bilateral in 10%. Feels soft and cystic. Benign, very unlikely to recur despite being multifocal, associated with smoking.
History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools. Long history, no pain, and no facial nerve involvement suggest benign tumour.

Surgery of the major salivary glands is primarily for tumours, obstruction, and, less commonly, inflammatory conditions. With the exception of lymphomas all salivary gland tumours should have surgery initially, patient permitting.
